trial_name: PROPPR — Transfusion of Plasma, Platelets, and Red Blood Cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 Ratio and Mortality in Patients With Severe Trauma (2015)
citation: Holcomb JB, Tilley BC, Baraniuk S, et al; PROPPR Study Group. Transfusion of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 ratio and mortality in patients with severe trauma: the PROPPR randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(5):471-482.
trial_type: RCT — pragmatic, phase 3, multicenter, open-label, superiority
one_liner: In severely injured trauma patients predicted to need massive transfusion, a 1:1:1 plasma:platelets:RBC ratio did not significantly reduce 24-hour or 30-day all-cause mortality compared with 1:1:2, but significantly decreased 24-hour exsanguination deaths and increased achievement of anatomic hemostasis.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients (age >=15 years or weight >=50 kg) admitted directly from the injury scene with severe trauma and predicted to require massive transfusion who received >=1 unit of blood component.
pico.intervention: Transfusion strategy targeting a 1:1:1 ratio of plasma:platelets:RBC (1 unit plasma + 1 platelet dose + 1 unit RBC) delivered via pre-packed blood bank containers during active hemorrhage resuscitation.
pico.comparison: Transfusion strategy targeting a 1:1:2 ratio of plasma:platelets:RBC (1 unit plasma + 1 platelet dose + 2 units RBC) delivered via pre-packed blood bank containers.
pico.outcome: Co-primary endpoints: All-cause mortality at 24 hours and 30 days.

related_trials: European guidance on traumatic major bleeding

background.existing_knowledge: Hemorrhage is a leading early cause of death after severe trauma. Damage control resuscitation emphasizing early, higher plasma and platelet ratios alongside RBCs was increasingly adopted based on observational data.
background.knowledge_gap: Observational evidence was limited by survival bias and confounding. Resuscitation practice varied widely (including RBC-heavy early protocols and delayed platelets), and safety concerns persisted regarding inflammatory, volume-related, and thrombotic complications.
background.hypothesis: In adults with severe trauma predicted to require massive transfusion, a 1:1:1 plasma:platelets:RBC ratio during active hemorrhage resuscitation reduces 24-hour and 30-day all-cause mortality compared with a 1:1:2 strategy without increasing adverse safety events.

methods.design: Pragmatic, phase 3, multisite, randomized, open-label clinical trial with site-stratified randomization at container seal break.
methods.setting: 12 Level I trauma centers in North America; emergency department activations for highest-level trauma.

inclusion: Received >=1 unit of blood component within 1 hour of arrival or during prehospital transport
exclusion: Devastating traumatic brain injury (GCS 3 with head AIS >=5)
Expected death within 1 hour of ED admission
Fourth unit of RBC transfused prior to randomization

methods.intervention: 1:1:1 strategy targeting 1 unit plasma + 1 platelet dose + 1 unit RBC issued sequentially in blood bank coolers. First cooler targeted within 10 minutes of request and continued during active bleeding until anatomic hemostasis or protocol cessation.
methods.comparison: 1:1:2 strategy targeting 1 unit plasma + 1 platelet dose + 2 units RBC issued in sequential blood bank coolers (platelets delivered later relative to RBCs).
methods.blinding: Unblinded at bedside due to visible blood product differences. Mortality endpoints objective; cause of death adjudicated.
methods.sample_size_power: Initially planned sample size of 580 to detect a 10% absolute reduction in 24-hour mortality (21% to 11%, 90% power, alpha 0.044 adjusted for interim analyses) and 12% absolute reduction in 30-day mortality (35% to 23%, 88% power). Randomized 680 patients total.
methods.primary_outcome: Co-primary endpoints: All-cause mortality at 24 hours and 30 days post-injury.
secondary_outcomes: Death due to exsanguination within 24 hours
Time to death due to exsanguination
Total blood products transfused at 24 hours
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) to 30 days
Venous thromboembolism (DVT or PE) to 30 days

headline_bullets: No statistically significant difference in co-primary all-cause mortality at 24 hours (12.7% vs 17.0%, adjusted RR 0.75) or 30 days (22.4% vs 26.1%, adjusted RR 0.85).
Significant reduction in 24-hour deaths due to exsanguination with 1:1:1 (9.2% vs 14.6%, P=0.03).
Significantly higher rate of achieved anatomic hemostasis with 1:1:1 (86.1% vs 78.1%, P=0.006).
Total blood products transfused at 24 hours were higher with 1:1:1 (median 25.5 vs 19.0 units, P<0.001) without increasing 30-day complications (ARDS, organ failure, VTE).

outcomes_table.note: Risk difference −3.7% (95% CI −10.2 to 2.7); 4 patients missing 30-day status (3 vs 1)

outcomes_table.outcome: Death due to exsanguination within 24 h
outcomes_table.note: Mean time to exsanguination death: 105.7 ± 73.8 vs 96.1 ± 68.7 min (P=0.50)
Defined by surgeon in OR or resolution of contrast blush on IR angiography

outcomes_table.outcome: Total blood products to 24 h after admission
outcomes_table.note: Values are median (IQR); includes pre-randomization, intervention, and post-intervention periods
No excess organ failure signal with higher plasma/platelet delivery

outcomes_table.outcome: Venous thromboembolism (DVT or PE to 30 d)

safety: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) to 30 days: 7.2% in 1:1:1 vs 5.6% in 1:1:2 (P=0.42; RD 1.6%, 95% CI -2.2 to 5.4)
Multiple organ failure to 30 days: 9.8% in 1:1:1 vs 9.1% in 1:1:2 (P=0.79; RD 0.7%, 95% CI -3.8 to 5.2)
Venous thromboembolism (DVT or PE) to 30 days: 8.0% in 1:1:1 vs 9.4% in 1:1:2 (P=0.53; RD -1.4%, 95% CI -5.8 to 2.9)
No signal for excess inflammatory, infectious, or volume-overload complications with higher plasma and platelet exposure

domains.notes: Site-stratified randomization executed via blood bank pre-packed coolers; allocation randomized at container seal break.
Unblinded delivery at bedside due to visible product physical differences. Primary mortality endpoints were objective; cause of death required committee adjudication.

680 randomized (338 in 1:1:1; 342 in 1:1:2); 669 received randomized products. Primary ITT analysis; 24h mortality complete; 30d status missing in 4 patients (3 vs 1). GOS-E recorded in small subset (30 vs 28).

Products transfused out of order: 4% (1:1:1) vs 7% (1:1:2) (P=0.01). Active phase separation achieved: median plasma:RBC ratio 1.0 vs 0.5, platelets:RBC ratio 1.5 vs 0.4. Platelets given to 98.5% vs 59.9%. Post-protocol care at clinician discretion.

Groups well-matched: ISS 26.5 vs 26; SBP <=90 mm Hg in 38.5% vs 39.8%; base excess -8.0 ± 7.6 vs -8.5 ± 7.7. TXA use: 18.9% vs 19.9%. Non-TXA procoagulants: 5.6% vs 4.4%. True massive transfusion (>=10 RBC units in 24h): 45.3% vs 46.8%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong, supported by pragmatic site-stratified randomization, complete primary follow-up, objective endpoints, and clear operational protocol separation during active resuscitation.

domains.notes: High-acuity trauma population: median age 34 years; 75% male; blunt trauma 51–55%, penetrating 45–49%; shock physiology in ~40%. Excluded severe TBI (GCS 3 with head AIS >=5), burns >20%, pregnancy, CPR >5 min, and emergency thoracotomy.

Highly applicable to mature Level I trauma centers with 24/7 blood bank capabilities for issuing thawed plasma and platelets in pre-packed coolers within 10 minutes. Less generalizable to resource-limited settings or systems utilizing prehospital whole blood.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate-to-high for major trauma centers operating massive transfusion protocols with rapid component availability, but limited for excluded severe TBI phenotypes and low-resource settings.

strengths: Large pragmatic multicenter RCT addressing time-critical trauma resuscitation
Operationally realistic intervention using pre-packed blood bank coolers issued rapidly (median ED arrival to randomization ~26–28 min)
Prespecified co-primary endpoints with high completeness of mortality follow-up
Demonstrated clear operational separation in plasma and platelet delivery ratios without increasing safety complications
limitations: Unblinded design with risk of co-intervention differences post-protocol phase
All-cause mortality endpoint susceptible to dilution from non-hemorrhagic deaths (e.g., severe TBI)
Only 45–47% of enrolled patients ultimately required >=10 units of RBCs in 24 hours (imperfect prognostic enrichment)
Functional outcome data (GOS-E) collected in only a small exploratory subset (n=58 total)

critical_appraisal.summary: PROPPR is a landmark, high-quality pragmatic RCT demonstrating that early 1:1:1 component resuscitation improves early hemostasis and reduces 24-hour exsanguination deaths without increasing organ failure or thrombotic complications, despite neutral all-cause mortality.
strengths: High adherence to component ratio delivery during active hemorrhage phase
Objective primary endpoints with systematic complication tracking
weaknesses: Potential dilution of primary endpoint by non-bleeding causes of death
Incomplete prognostic enrichment with over half of participants receiving <10 RBC units

sections.authors_conclusion: Among patients with severe trauma and predicted massive transfusion, a 1:1:1 ratio compared with 1:1:2 did not result in significant differences in 24-hour or 30-day mortality. However, 1:1:1 resulted in more patients achieving hemostasis and fewer deaths due to exsanguination at 24 hours, with no safety differences.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Supports early balanced component resuscitation (1:1:1 plasma:platelets:RBC) as the preferred initial strategy in massive transfusion protocols to improve early hemostasis and reduce early exsanguination.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult trauma patients admitted direct from scene with severe injury and predicted need for massive transfusion.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not prove an overall 30-day all-cause mortality benefit, nor does it establish superiority of ratio-based component therapy over cold-stored whole blood or viscoelastic-guided resuscitation.
implementation_caveats: Requires blood bank infrastructure capable of preparing thawed plasma and platelets in cooler containers within 10 minutes
Massive transfusion protocol activation criteria must balance rapid deployment against blood component wastage, given ~54% non-massive transfusion rate

controversies.topic: Primary endpoint neutrality vs secondary benefit
controversies.notes: Co-primary all-cause mortality was statistically neutral, sparking debate regarding whether secondary reductions in exsanguination deaths represented true treatment effect or selective over-interpretation.

A subsequent Bayesian re-analysis demonstrated a high posterior probability of mortality benefit for 1:1:1, challenging rigid frequentist interpretations in heterogeneous emergency resuscitation trials.
Fixed component ratio strategies are increasingly compared against cold-stored whole blood, prehospital plasma, and viscoelastic-guided (TEG/ROTEM) resuscitation.

context_related_trials.trial: European guidance on traumatic major bleeding
context_related_trials.relation: Incorporated PROPPR trial evidence to endorse early balanced blood component resuscitation within damage control protocols.

unresolved_questions: Comparative efficacy and safety of 1:1:1 component resuscitation vs low-titer O negative whole blood
Impact of prehospital plasma and RBC transfusion prior to MTP activation
Optimal transition point from fixed ratio-based resuscitation to viscoelastic-guided goal-directed therapy

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: 1:1:1 transfusion does not significantly improve 30-day all-cause survival over 1:1:2, but reduces early exsanguination deaths and improves hemostasis without increasing complications.
